                                                        Abstract
      Hypothesis selection asks for a distribution close to an unknown P , given samples from P and
      access to n candidate hypotheses.We study the computational complexity of achieving statistically
      optimal sample complexity and approximation factors. 1
      Keywords: Hypothesis selection, density estimation, distribution learning
    Given sample access to an unknown distribution P and sample/query access to hypotheses H =
{H1 , . . . , Hn } over a (possibly infinite) domain X , the goal is to output Q with dTV (P, Q) ≤
C · OPT + ε, where OPT = mini dTV (P, Hi ). With O(log(n/δ)/ε2 ) samples from P , proper
algorithms achieve the tight factor C = 3, while statistically optimal improper algorithms can
achieve C = 2 but previously known implementations have runtimes which depend polynomially
on |X | (Bousquet et al., 2019, 2021). We investigate whether optimal statistical guarantees admit
domain-independent, near-linear time algorithms.
Mixture outputs. A natural finite-time improper strategy outputs a mixture of the hypotheses.
We prove the exact optimal factor 3 − 2/n for such outputs: we give a lower bound for every
domain-independent-sample algorithm and a matching algorithm which runs in poly(n) time. Thus
mixtures recover the known C = 2 guarantee for n = 2 (Mahalanabis and Stefankovic, 2008), but
cannot yield an absolute constant below 3 for general n.
Proper near-linear time. For proper hypothesis selection with optimal factor C = 3, the previous
fastest algorithms run in time O(n2 log(n/δ)/ε2 ) and Õ(n/(δ 3 ε3 )) (Mahalanabis and Stefankovic,
2008; Aliakbarpour et al., 2024). We improve the latter result to Õ(n/(δε2 )) while retaining optimal
sample complexity. Our algorithm reduces the task to a graph problem and solves it using ideas from
sublinear graph algorithms to avoid comparing all Θ(n2 ) pairs of hypotheses.
Additional resources. Given an upper bound R ≥ OPT, we obtain runtime O(n log3 (n/δ)/ε2 ),
and output Hi with dTV (P, Hi ) ≤ 2OPT + R + ε. When R = OPT, this gives C = 3 without a
polynomial dependence on 1/δ. For finite domains when polynomial preprocessing of H is allowed,
we give a data structure with C = 3 and Õ(n2−Ω(ε) ε−3 ) query time which succeeds with high
probability in n. In both settings, our algorithms utilize the extra resources to break the quadratic
barrier for high probability selection with the optimal approximation.
